newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh expects peace deal with rebels soon.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh expects peace deal with rebels soon.

text.p: Bangladesh expects a much awaited peace agreement to end tribal insurgency in the Chittagong Hill Tracts to be signed next month despite opposition by militant tribal students, state officials said on Thursday.
"We expect the next round of talks in Dhaka on July 14 with the political wing of (tribal) Shanti Bahini guerrillas will lead to a formal agreement for peace," one official told Reuters.
He said the government had accepted an offer by the rebels that a truce in the 5,500 sq-mile (14,200 sq-km) Hill Tracts, due to expire on Monday, to be extended to September 30.
"The government sincerely wants peace following a protracted insurgency that has cost lives, fuelled ethnic rivalries and delayed development," said the official, who declined to be named.
The Shanti Bahini began the insurgency in 1973 after Bangladesh rejected its demand for autonomy for the Hill Tracts, which borders India and Burma.
They also want some 500,000 Bengali-speaking settlers to be removed from the region.
More than 8,500 people including rebels, soldiers and civilians have been killed in the insurgency, which also forced some 50,000 tribespeople to flee to northeast India.
Nearly 7,000 tribal refugees returned home in March and April following an agreement between Dhaka and New Delhi, and officials expect the next phase of repatriation to begin in July.

They said broad outlines of the peace agreement had already been reached at talks between the Parbatya Chattagram Jana Sanghati Samity (PCJSS), the political arm of the Shantis, and the government in May.
"The formal signing of the agreement is expected during the next round (of talks) or shortly after that," one official said.

But the Hill Students Federation (HSF), believed to have strong links with the hard-core section of the Shanti Bahini, opposes any deal that would not guarantee "enough autonomy" for the Hill Tracts, which they consider a tribal homeland.

"The HSF has been a constant threat to peace efforts but we hope to overcome it as the majority section of the rebels and their political mentors have now realised that the insurgency would achieve them nothing," a state official told Reuters.
Another was not so sure, but said "peace now had a brighter prospect" because India, which allegedly helped the Shanti Bahini for decades, recently withdrew its support.

"That India and Bangladesh have recently agreed to help each other in combating insurgencies along their borders gives a clear signal to Shanti Bahini to pack up and seek out peace," one Hill Tracts analyst said.
"Now it's a matter of time only," he added.
